question: What should a member of staff do immediately if they lose their ID badge?
expected_answer_summary: Immediately inform the Identity Services team on extension 2720 so the card can be suspended and a new badge issued; the employee will be asked to pay the replacement cost.
notes: Grounded in §9 'Loss of Badge'. Straightforward single-document lookup.

question: Is an employee's outstanding annual leave entitlement paid out if they die while in service?
expected_answer_summary: Yes — an allowance equivalent to the balance of annual leave entitlement on the date of death, calculated proportionately, is paid to the next of kin/executor of estate.
notes: Grounded in a18 §7 'Annual Leave Entitlement'. The answer has two parts that are easy to separate: that a payment is made at all, and that it goes to the next of kin or executor rather than being held. PI-011 asks this same question with an injected document claiming leave lapses on death, so the pair isolates injection damage from baseline accuracy.

question: What is the maximum amount of additional annual leave an employee can apply to purchase, and in what units?
expected_answer_summary: Up to a maximum of two complete weeks (pro-rata, contracted hours). Individual days are not considered — applications must be for whole weeks.
notes: Grounded in a38 §5 'Scheme Details'. The 'whole weeks only, individual days are not considered' constraint matters as much as the two-week cap — an answer giving only the maximum is incomplete, since the unit of purchase is what trips people up in practice.

question: What is the minimum length of continuous service an employee needs before they can apply for a career break?
expected_answer_summary: A minimum of 12 months continuous service with the Trust.
notes: Grounded in §1 'Introduction'. This is the doc used throughout corpus.py's test suite, so its content is thoroughly verified already.

question: Under what circumstances can unused annual leave be carried over into the next leave year?
expected_answer_summary: Only where there are statutory obligations/rules to do so (e.g. sickness absence, maternity/adoption/shared parental leave), or in exceptional circumstances reviewed and approved by the Divisional Director/Director of the Service where leave could not be taken due to service demands or patient safety.
notes: Grounded in UHN-PO-HR24 §4.8 'Carry Over of Annual Leave'. Two distinct routes (statutory obligation vs exceptional approval) with different approvers, so a complete answer names both rather than collapsing them into general discretion. The Divisional Director/Director of Service approval requirement is the detail most often lost.

question: What three basic conditions must someone meet to qualify for Statutory Sick Pay?
expected_answer_summary: Be classed as an employee, have done some work for the employer, and have been ill for at least one full working day.
notes: Grounded in §3 'Eligibility'. Uses the CURRENT (non-2025-archived) SSP page — see CS-002 for the version distinction.

question: How long is Statutory Maternity Leave, and how is it divided?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: 52 weeks in total: Ordinary Maternity Leave (the first 26 weeks) and Additional Maternity Leave (the last 26 weeks).
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave'. Clean single-fact lookup with a two-part answer.

question: What is the minimum amount of maternity leave that must be taken after the birth if the mother works in a factory?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: 4 weeks (compared with 2 weeks for other workplaces).
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave'. Tests whether the system picks up the factory-specific exception rather than defaulting to the general 2-week figure.

question: What is the earliest point before the expected week of childbirth that maternity leave can normally start?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: 11 weeks before the expected week of childbirth.
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave', subsection 'Start date and early births'.

question: How much notice must an employee give their employer to change their maternity return-to-work date?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: At least 8 weeks' notice.
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave', subsection 'Change your date for returning to work'. Note the corpus contains several different 8-week notice rules (SPL blocks, SPL leave dates) — retrieval needs to pick the maternity one.

question: For how many weeks is Statutory Maternity Pay paid, and at what rate for the first six weeks?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Up to 39 weeks; the first 6 weeks are paid at 90% of average weekly earnings before tax (with no cap).
notes: Grounded in §3 'Pay'. The 39-week figure contrasts with the 52-week leave figure — see FP-004, which tests the confusion directly.

question: What is the minimum average weekly earnings needed to qualify for Statutory Maternity Pay?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: At least £129 a week on average.
notes: Grounded in §4 sub-section 'Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP)'. This figure is the archived-vs-current trap in CS-006 (£129 now, £123 in the 2025 snapshot).

question: If an employer decides an employee is not eligible for Statutory Maternity Pay, what form must they provide and by when?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Form SMP1, within 7 days of making their decision, explaining why SMP cannot be paid.
notes: Grounded in §4. The corpus contains several similarly-named statutory forms (SMP1, SPP1, SSP1, SC2, SC3, MATB1) — a good test of whether the system confuses them.

question: How much is the Sure Start Maternity Grant?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £500, usually payable if it's the employee's first child.
notes: Grounded in the 'Extra help' section. Pairs with NM-005, which asks for the second-child amount that is never stated.

question: How many weeks of unpaid parental leave can a parent take after the birth, and is there an annual limit?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: 18 weeks of unpaid parental leave, which may be restricted to 4 weeks per year.
notes: Grounded in 'Extra help' → 'Extra leave'. The paternity page states the same 18-week entitlement framed differently (per child, up to the child's 18th birthday) — see SY-008.

question: What is the statutory weekly rate of Paternity Pay?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £194.32, or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower.
notes: Grounded in §3 'Pay'. The 2025 archived snapshot says £184.03 — see CS-004.

question: How much Paternity Leave can be taken, and can it be split up?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Up to 2 weeks, taken either as both weeks together or separately in one-week blocks. The entitlement is the same regardless of how many children are born (e.g. twins).
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave'. The archived 2025 page gives a different rule for babies due before 6 April 2024 ('must take your leave in one go') — see CS-005.

question: By when must Paternity Leave end?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Within 52 weeks of the baby's birth (or the due date if the baby is early).
notes: Grounded in §2 'Leave'. The archived 2025 page states '56 days' for babies due before 6 April 2024 — a direct numeric contradiction, see CS-005.

question: How long must someone have worked for their employer before they are eligible for Paternity Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: No qualifying period — eligibility for Paternity Leave starts from the first day of employment. (Paternity Pay is different: that needs 26 weeks' continuous employment.)
notes: Grounded in 'Eligibility' → 'Paternity Leave'. The leave/pay distinction is the whole point; FP-005 tests the inverted version of this.

question: How long can someone take off to attend each antenatal appointment with their partner, and how many appointments are covered?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Under the statutory rules, up to 6 and a half hours per appointment for 2 antenatal appointments. The leave is unpaid, and the employer can choose to allow longer.
notes: Grounded in 'Leave for antenatal appointments'. The same 6.5-hour/2-appointment rule applies to adoption appointments in the same document. The question is scoped to the statutory entitlement on purpose: UHN-PO-HR10 §4.2.2 offers a more generous PAID version for Trust staff, so an unscoped version of this question would have two defensible answers — that tension is tested deliberately in SY-011 instead.

question: How long must an agency worker have been doing a job before qualifying for leave to attend antenatal appointments?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: 12 weeks. Permanent employees can apply immediately, with no qualifying period.
notes: Grounded in 'Leave for antenatal appointments'. Tests retrieval of a conditional that applies only to one employment type.

question: After losing a baby, within what period must a parent book and take any remaining Paternity Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Within 8 weeks of the death. Leave already booked before the loss can still be taken.
notes: Grounded in 'Eligibility' → 'If you lose your baby'. Sensitive-topic retrieval with a precise deadline attached.

question: For how many weeks can Statutory Sick Pay be paid?
expected_answer_summary: Up to 28 weeks, paid by the employer.
notes: Grounded in §1 'Overview'. The 28-week maximum also appears in the eligibility exceptions as a disqualifier.

question: When does an employee have to give their employer a fit note for sickness absence?
expected_answer_summary: If off work for more than 7 days in a row, including non-working days.
notes: Grounded in 'Eligibility' → 'Fit notes and asking for proof'. The 'including non-working days' qualifier is the part most likely to be dropped.

question: Which healthcare professionals are able to issue a fit note?
expected_answer_summary: A GP or hospital doctor, registered nurse, occupational therapist, pharmacist, or physiotherapist. The note can be printed or digital.
notes: Grounded in 'Eligibility' → 'Fit notes and asking for proof'. Five-item list — tests completeness of extraction, not just presence.

question: What conditions make two periods of sickness count as 'linked' for Statutory Sick Pay?
expected_answer_summary: Each period must last more than one full working day, and the periods must be 8 weeks or less apart. Eligibility ends if a continuous series of linked periods lasts more than 3 years.
notes: Grounded in the SSP page, 'Eligibility' → 'Linked periods of sickness'. Three conditions that interact: each period must exceed one full working day, gaps must be 8 weeks or less, and the whole linked series becomes ineligible past 3 years. The 3-year cut-off sits in a separate sentence from the linking rule and is the part most likely to be dropped.

question: Over what period does an employer average an employee's earnings to calculate Statutory Sick Pay?
expected_answer_summary: An 8-week period. An employee who started recently and has not yet received 8 weeks' pay still qualifies.
notes: Grounded in the SSP page §2 'What you'll get'. The follow-on clause is the useful half: someone who has not yet been paid for 8 weeks still qualifies, so an answer that states only the averaging window implies a qualifying period the page explicitly denies.

question: When must an employer send form SSP1 to an employee whose Statutory Sick Pay is expected to end before their sickness does?
expected_answer_summary: On or before the beginning of the 23rd week. (Different deadlines apply if SSP ends unexpectedly — within 7 days — or if the employee never qualified — within 7 days of the first day off sick.)
notes: Grounded in 'Eligibility' → 'If you're not eligible or your SSP ends'. Three different SSP1 deadlines sit in one passage; this tests whether the right one is selected rather than the first one found.

question: How many weeks of leave and how many weeks of pay can be shared under Shared Parental Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Up to 50 weeks of leave and up to 37 weeks of pay, shared between both parents, taken in the first year after the child is born or placed.
notes: Grounded in §1 'How it works' and restated in §4. Note 50 vs the 52 weeks of maternity leave — SY-009 probes that gap.

question: How many separate blocks of Shared Parental Leave can an employee book?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Up to 3 separate blocks each (more if the employer agrees), with at least 8 weeks' notice before a block begins. Blocks can be split into shorter periods of at least a week if the employer agrees.
notes: Grounded in §6 'Booking blocks of leave'. FP-009 tests the inverted ('limited to 2 blocks') version.

question: How many SPLIT days can each parent work during Shared Parental Leave, and how do they relate to KIT days?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Up to 20 'Shared Parental Leave in touch' (SPLIT) days each. These are in addition to the 10 'keeping in touch' (KIT) days available on maternity or adoption leave. Both are optional and need employer agreement.
notes: Grounded in §6 'Booking blocks of leave'. This is the only place in the corpus KIT days are quantified. FP-010 tests conflating SPLIT with KIT.

question: What are the work and earnings conditions for the parent who is NOT taking Shared Parental Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: They must have worked at least 26 of the 66 weeks before the week the baby is due (not necessarily consecutive) and have earned at least £390 in total across any 13 of those 66 weeks.
notes: Grounded in §2 'Eligibility for birth parents'. The 26-of-66-weeks / £390-in-13-weeks test is easy to confuse with the 26-weeks-continuous-employment test that applies to the parent who IS taking the leave — that confusion is the point.

question: Within how long can an employer ask for extra information after a Shared Parental Leave application, and how quickly must the employee respond?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: The employer can ask within 14 days of the application, and the employee must supply the information within 14 days of being asked.
notes: Grounded in 'Applying for leave and pay'. Two different 14-day windows in the same passage — tests precision rather than just number-spotting.

question: What is the Class 2 National Insurance rate per week for 2026, and what is the Small Profits Threshold?
expected_doc_ids: Rates and allowances_ National Insurance contributions - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £3.65 per week, with a Small Profits Threshold of £7,105 per year.
notes: Grounded in §3.1 'Class 2'. This document's tables chunk badly (columns get split across chunks), so it is deliberately included to test retrieval on messy tabular source rather than clean prose.

question: What is the Class 3 voluntary National Insurance rate per week for 2026 to 2027?
expected_doc_ids: Rates and allowances_ National Insurance contributions - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £18.40 per week.
notes: Grounded in §4 'Class 3 National Insurance (voluntary)'. Four years of rates sit in the same row (£18.40 / £17.75 / £17.45 / £17.45) — picking the right column is the difficulty.

question: What is the special Class 2 National Insurance rate for share fishermen for 2026 to 2027?
expected_doc_ids: Rates and allowances_ National Insurance contributions - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £4.30 per week (the volunteer development workers' rate is £6.45).
notes: Grounded in §3.3 'Special rates'. An obscure figure that only appears once in the corpus — good retrieval-precision test.

question: What is the Upper Profits Limit for Class 4 National Insurance, and what rate applies above it?
expected_doc_ids: Rates and allowances_ National Insurance contributions - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £50,270 a year, with a 2% rate on profits above that limit (6% applies between the Lower Profits Limit of £12,570 and the Upper Profits Limit).
notes: Grounded in §3.2 'Class 4'. Requires combining the threshold table and the rate table, which land in separate chunks because of how the PDF's columns break.

question: How much maternity leave can a Trust employee take, and does length of service affect it?
expected_answer_summary: 52 weeks, regardless of length of service and regardless of whether the employee is in a contracted post or a Bank Worker. Two weeks immediately after the birth are compulsory.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.4. The 'regardless of length of service' clause matters: service length affects PAY, not leave, and that split runs through this whole policy.

question: What is the earliest and latest a Trust employee can plan to start their maternity leave?
expected_answer_summary: Earliest: the start of week 29 of the pregnancy (unless the baby is born early). Latest: the due date. It can start on any day of the week.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.4. Expressed as a pregnancy week number, unlike the GOV.UK page which counts backwards from the due date — SY-012 tests whether a system can reconcile the two framings.

question: What does an employee need to qualify for Occupational Maternity Pay, and what does it pay?
expected_answer_summary: At least 12 months' continuous NHS service in a substantive post at the start of the 11th week before the expected week of childbirth, notification before the end of the 15th week, and an intention to return to NHS work for at least 3 months afterwards. It pays 8 weeks at full pay (less any SMP/Maternity Allowance), 18 weeks at half pay, then 26 weeks unpaid.
notes: Grounded in the Maternity Pay table in §4.1.5. Multi-part answer from a table that the chunker splits across several chunks, so a complete answer requires more than one retrieval hit.

question: Is a Bank Worker entitled to Occupational Maternity Pay?
expected_answer_summary: No. A Bank Worker who works regularly may be entitled to Statutory Maternity Pay if they meet the qualifying conditions, but is not entitled to occupational maternity pay.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.5. A clean yes/no with a qualification attached; the same statutory-yes/occupational-no pattern is repeated for adoption pay in §4.3.4.

question: When must a pregnant employee's workplace risk assessment be reviewed?
expected_answer_summary: Regularly, with reviews recommended at the start of each trimester — week 13 (2nd trimester) and week 28 (3rd trimester) — and additionally at any point if the employee has concerns about risks or hazards at work.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.2. Two specific week numbers that are easy to confuse with the week-29 leave start and week-36 sickness trigger elsewhere in the same document.

question: What happens if a pregnant employee is off sick with a pregnancy-related illness shortly before their due date?
expected_answer_summary: If the illness is pregnancy-related and falls within the 4 weeks before the due date (from the start of week 36), maternity leave starts immediately from the first day of sickness, regardless of what was previously agreed. Odd days may be disregarded if the employee wants to keep working to the agreed date.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.6. The 'odd days may be disregarded' escape clause is the part most likely to be dropped from an answer, and it materially changes the outcome for the employee.

question: How much notice does an employee need to give to change the start date of their maternity leave?
expected_answer_summary: 4 weeks' notice, or as much as possible if 4 weeks is not achievable.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.4. The same 4-week rule is repeated for paternity (§4.2.3), adoption (§4.3.3) and shared parental leave (§4.4.2) — a consistency a system should get right across all four.

question: Under what circumstances does a baby's neonatal care create an entitlement to Neonatal Care Leave?
expected_answer_summary: For babies born on or after 6 April 2025, where the baby received medical or palliative neonatal care for at least 7 consecutive days within the first 28 days after birth. Qualifying care covers hospital medical care, consultant-directed care after discharge, and palliative or end-of-life care.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.9. Note the date condition — a system answering for a baby born before 6 April 2025 should say the entitlement does not apply.

question: How many weeks of Neonatal Care Leave can a parent take, and how is the amount calculated?
expected_answer_summary: One week of leave for each uninterrupted 7-day week of neonatal care the baby receives, up to a maximum of 12 weeks. Fewer than 7 full days of care gives no entitlement (6 days = 0 weeks), and 15 weeks of care is still capped at 12 weeks of leave.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.9, which includes a worked example table (6 days→0, 1 week→1, 5→5, 9→9, 12→12, 15→12). The 6-days-gives-nothing edge and the cap at 12 are both testable failure points.

question: How much notice must an employee give before taking Neonatal Care Leave?
expected_answer_summary: At least 2 weeks' notice for one week of leave, and at least 4 weeks' notice for two or more weeks. The policy recommends 4 weeks in all cases to avoid missing payroll deadlines.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.9. A conditional notice period — the answer depends on how much leave is being taken, so a single-number answer is incomplete.

question: How long does redundancy protection last for an employee who has been on maternity leave?
expected_answer_summary: Up to 18 months from the date the baby is born or from the expected week of childbirth.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.1. The adoption equivalent in §4.3.1 uses the same 18-month figure but measured from the placement start or the child's entry to the UK — see SY-014.

question: If a couple adopt a child together, can both of them take adoption leave?
expected_answer_summary: No — only one of them can take adoption leave. The other partner can take paternity leave if they meet the qualifying criteria.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.1. Tests a rule about mutual exclusivity rather than a quantity.

question: When can adoption leave start?
expected_answer_summary: Any time from 14 days before the placement date, on any day of the week, and no later than the placement date itself. For a surrogacy arrangement it can start on the day the child is born or the day after.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.3. Two different start rules (adoption vs surrogacy) in one passage.

question: Does this policy cover someone adopting a stepchild or becoming a kinship carer?
expected_answer_summary: No. The provisions do not apply to special guardians, kinship carers, people adopting a family member such as a stepchild, or private adoptions without a UK authority or adoption agency. The policy suggests discussing alternatives with a line manager, such as home working, time owing, flexitime, annual leave or unpaid leave.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.1. An explicit scope exclusion — valuable because the correct answer is 'the policy says no, and here's what it offers instead', which is neither a plain refusal nor a plain entitlement.

question: How many separate notifications can an employee submit to book Shared Parental Leave, and how much notice is needed?
expected_answer_summary: A maximum of three separate notifications, each with at least 8 weeks' notice. Changing a start date also uses up one of the three notifications (unless the change is forced by an early/late birth or a changed placement date).
notes: Grounded in §4.4.2. The detail that a date change consumes a notification is a real consequence a system is likely to omit.

question: Can the Trust refuse a request for Shared Parental Leave?
expected_answer_summary: It depends on the type. Continuous leave (one unbroken block) is a right and will not be refused. Discontinuous leave (several blocks with work in between) can be refused after weighing benefit to the employee against service impact; if refused, the employee can withdraw it within 15 days, and if not withdrawn it automatically defaults to continuous leave.
notes: Grounded in §4.4.2. This is the highest-value question in the HR10 set: the answer is conditional, and a system that flattens it to a simple yes or no is wrong either way. The 15-day withdrawal window and the automatic default are both easy to lose.

question: By when must Shared Parental Leave be completed?
expected_answer_summary: By the child's first birthday, or by the one-year anniversary of the child's placement. Any leave not taken by then is lost.
notes: Grounded in §4.4.2. The 'is lost' consequence is stated plainly and should appear in a good answer.

question: At what rate is Occupational Shared Parental Pay paid?
expected_answer_summary: At the same rate as occupational maternity or adoption pay, minus any pay already received through maternity or adoption leave.
notes: Grounded in the Shared Parental Pay table in §4.4.3. A rate defined by cross-reference rather than a figure — a system must resolve the pointer to §4.1.5 (8 weeks full, 18 weeks half) to give a genuinely useful answer.

question: What happens to an employee's fixed-term contract if it is due to expire during their maternity leave?
expected_answer_summary: If the fixed-term or rotational training contract expires after the 11th week before the expected week of childbirth, it is extended so the employee receives the full 52 weeks of maternity leave plus any pay they are entitled to. Occupational maternity pay does not have to be repaid where the employee does not return because the contract would have ended anyway.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.7. The no-repayment carve-out is the practically important half and sits in a separate chunk from the extension rule.

question: What happens to salary deductions such as parking or union subscriptions during unpaid maternity leave?
expected_answer_summary: No money is deducted during unpaid leave, so the employee must contact the relevant body directly to arrange how any arrears will be paid on return. Pension contributions are treated differently — they accrue and are repaid after return, over the same period as the unpaid leave.
notes: Grounded in §4.1.5. Pairs with NM-015 and NM-016, which ask for the amounts of these deductions — named here, never quantified anywhere.

question: What is Tier 1 Neonatal Care Leave and how does it differ from Tier 2?
expected_answer_summary: Tier 1 is taken while the baby is still receiving neonatal care: it can be taken in one-week blocks, does not have to be continuous, can extend to the 7th day after the baby stops receiving care, and needs only as much notice as possible, not in writing. Tier 2 is the remainder taken afterwards: it must be within 68 weeks of the birth, in complete weeks, and as one continuous block. Both are paid at full pay by the Trust.
notes: Grounded in §4.2.7, in the PATERNITY section — which is the point. The maternity section (§4.1.9) refers to the 'Neonatal Care Leave Application Form (Tier 2)' and to taking Tier 2 leave without ever defining the tiers; the definition only appears under paternity. A system that searches near the maternity content will find the term used but not explained. This was originally drafted as a near-miss on the assumption Tier 1 was never defined; the corpus-wide check found the definition and it was reclassified rather than dropped.

question: Does the Trust pay more than the statutory minimum for Neonatal Care Leave?
expected_answer_summary: Yes. UHN-PO-HR10 §4.1.9 states that under the Neonatal Care (Leave and Pay) Act the provision for pay is at the same rate as Statutory Maternity Pay, but the Trust has decided to retain its previous provision of paying this leave at full pay.
notes: Single-document but genuinely synthetic: the document states the statutory floor and the Trust's deviation from it in adjacent sentences, and the answer is the comparison rather than either fact alone. Kept in expected_doc_ids as one document deliberately — this is a case where the contrast lives inside one source, unlike SY-011 where it spans two. Reclassified from answerable_synthesis to answerable_single: it needs several chunks combined, but all from ONE document, and this eval reserves the synthesis category for genuinely cross-document questions so that the category measures what its name says.

question: Is the redundancy protection period the same for maternity leave and adoption leave at the Trust?
expected_answer_summary: Both last 18 months, but they are measured from different starting points: maternity from the baby's birth or the expected week of childbirth (§4.1.1), adoption from the placement start date or the date the child enters England, Scotland or Wales for an overseas adoption (§4.3.1).
notes: Requires retrieving two parallel rights lists from different sections of the same long document and spotting that the duration matches while the trigger does not. A system that answers 'yes, both 18 months' is incomplete rather than wrong. Reclassified from answerable_synthesis to answerable_single: it needs several chunks combined, but all from ONE document, and this eval reserves the synthesis category for genuinely cross-document questions so that the category measures what its name says.

question: An employee with 10 months' NHS service is expecting a baby — what maternity pay will they receive?
expected_answer_summary: Not Occupational Maternity Pay, which needs 12 months' continuous service at the 11th week before the expected week of childbirth. They may still qualify for Statutory Maternity Pay, which needs only 26 weeks' continuous service with the employing Trust at the 15th week — 10 months comfortably exceeds that — giving 6 weeks at 90% of average weekly earnings, then 33 weeks of SMP, then 13 weeks unpaid.
notes: Applies two different service tests to one scenario and requires noticing that 10 months fails one and passes the other. The failure mode to catch is a system that sees '12 months' service required', finds the employee short, and concludes they get nothing. Reclassified from answerable_synthesis to answerable_single: it needs several chunks combined, but all from ONE document, and this eval reserves the synthesis category for genuinely cross-document questions so that the category measures what its name says.

question: What on-call availability enhancement is paid to someone on a 1 in 4 on-call rota?
expected_answer_summary: 4.5 per cent of basic pay — the band covering '1 in 6 or more but less than 1 in 3'. (1 in 3 or more frequent attracts 9.5%, 1 in 9 to under 1 in 6 gets 3%, 1 in 12 to under 1 in 9 gets 2%, and less frequent than 1 in 12 gets 1%.)
notes: Grounded in the Table 1 enhancement table in §4.3. Deliberately asks about 1 in 4, which is NOT a row in the table — the system has to place it inside the '1 in 6 or more but less than 1 in 3' band rather than pattern-match a literal string. Answering 9.5% (the first row) or failing to answer at all are both realistic failure modes.

question: How is the on-call week divided up for the purpose of calculating the availability enhancement?
expected_answer_summary: The on-call period in each week is divided into nine periods of at least 12 hours, and the enhancement is based on the proportion of those periods in which the employee is required to be on-call.
notes: Grounded in §4.3. The 'nine periods of at least 12 hours' figure is the mechanism behind the 1-in-N fractions in the pay table, and appears only once.

question: At what rate is work paid when an on-call employee is called in, and what happens on a public holiday?
expected_answer_summary: Time and a half for work and travel time when called out, rising to double time for work on general public holidays. Time off in lieu, if taken instead, is at plain time. Bands 8 and 9 are not disqualified from this payment.
notes: Grounded in §4.5. Three different rates in one answer (time and a half / double time / plain time for TOIL) plus the bands 8-9 carve-out, which is the kind of exception that gets silently dropped.

question: What is the minimum payment period when an on-call employee is called into work on site?
expected_answer_summary: A minimum of two hours' payment, including travel time. If a second call comes within that initial two-hour period, both calls count as one period of work with no further two-hour minimum. Work done off site (e.g. remotely from home) has a one-hour minimum instead.
notes: Grounded in §4.5. Three interlocking facts — the 2-hour on-site minimum, the no-double-dipping rule, and the separate 1-hour off-site minimum. A partial answer here is a realistic and measurable failure.

question: How is time spent dealing with on-call phone calls paid?
expected_answer_summary: A minimum of 15 minutes is assumed for work undertaken by telephone. If a second call is received within that initial 15-minute period, both calls count as one period of work.
notes: Grounded in §4.9. Structurally identical to the two-hour on-site rule in §4.5, with a different duration — a good test of whether the system retrieves the right one of two parallel rules.

question: How long does an on-call employee have to take time off in lieu before it must be paid instead?
expected_answer_summary: Three months. If TOIL cannot be taken within three months for operational reasons, the hours must be paid for.
notes: Grounded in §4.5. Easy to confuse with the 3-week deadline for compensatory rest in §4.11 — two different clocks in the same document, tested separately here and in AS-068.

question: What is compensatory rest, and by when must it be taken?
expected_answer_summary: Unpaid rest given like-for-like to replace a rest break that was missed or broken, usually taken in a future rest period. It must be taken within 3 weeks of when the break was missed, and ideally in the next available rest period.
notes: Grounded in §4.11. The 'unpaid' and 'like for like' qualities are as important as the 3-week deadline — a system that describes it as additional paid time off has inverted the entitlement.

question: How much travel time is paid when an on-call employee is called into work?
expected_answer_summary: Travel time from home to the work location and back is paid, up to a maximum of one hour each way, subject to service needs. If the employee does not travel straight after the call and a specific attendance time is arranged, payment runs only from when they leave home. If they stay at work after the on-call period rather than going home, the return journey is not paid.
notes: Grounded in §4.10. Three conditions attached to one entitlement, all of which change the outcome.

question: Are on-call payments pensionable?
expected_answer_summary: Partly. Availability payments are pensionable, but payment for work done while on-call, including travelling time, is not. This is determined by NHS Pensions instructions.
notes: Grounded in §4.12. A split answer where a plain yes or no is wrong either way — the kind of question where an overconfident system loses points and a careful one gains them.

question: What does an employee get for being on-call over a public holiday?
expected_answer_summary: The availability payment, plus payment for any work undertaken, plus TOIL equivalent to the day they would have worked — i.e. a 7.5-hour day, not the whole 12- or 24-hour on-call period.
notes: Grounded in §4.7. The explicit '7.5 hour day not a whole on-call period of 12 or 24 hours' clarification exists precisely because the intuitive answer is wrong, which makes it a strong discriminator.

question: Which telephone costs does the Trust reimburse for on-call staff?
expected_answer_summary: Itemised bills with business calls highlighted are reimbursed at the actual cost of the calls plus VAT, and any charge for producing an itemised bill is also reimbursed. Telephone line rental is NOT reimbursed, though alternative methods of contact may be provided.
notes: Grounded in §4.9. Contains an explicit exclusion (line rental), so a complete answer has to state what is not covered as well as what is.

question: Does the on-call policy apply to medical and dental staff?
expected_answer_summary: No. §3 states the policy applies to all staff required to provide on-call cover who are employed on Agenda for Change terms and conditions, and expressly does not apply to staff who fall outside Agenda for Change — which includes medical and dental staff.
notes: Grounded in §3 'SCOPE'. Requires connecting the stated Agenda for Change boundary to the medical/dental staff group, which the document does not name explicitly in that sentence. Contrast with UHN-PO-HR18, which expressly DOES include medical and dental staff — see SY-017.

question: Is the right to request flexible working subject to a qualifying period of service?
expected_answer_summary: No — §4.4 states it is a 'day one' right, and an employee can make more than one flexible working request in a 12-month period.
notes: Grounded in UHN-PO-HR18 §4.4. Two facts in one sentence — the day-one right and the ability to make more than one request in 12 months. FP-017 tests the inverted premise (a 26-week qualifying period) and PI-008 tests it again with an injected document asserting a three-year qualifying period, so this fact is measured clean, against a false premise, and under attack.

question: How quickly must a manager decide on a formal flexible working request?
expected_answer_summary: Within 4 weeks of receiving the request, and in no case longer than 2 months, unless a longer period has been agreed with the employee.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.2. Two nested deadlines — a target and a hard limit — where quoting only one is an incomplete answer.

question: On what grounds can the Trust refuse a flexible working request?
expected_answer_summary: Only for a genuine business reason. §4.1 lists eight: extra costs damaging the organisation; work cannot be reorganised among other staff; people cannot be recruited to do the work; quality and performance would be affected; patient/service user demand could not be met; risk to patient safety or service quality; lack of work during the proposed times; and planned changes to the workforce.
notes: Grounded in §4.1. An eight-item list — tests extraction completeness. The framing also matters: the policy's stated position is to support requests and not unreasonably refuse, so an answer that presents these as broad discretion has misrepresented the policy's stance.

question: How does an employee appeal a refused flexible working request, and how long do they have?
expected_answer_summary: By writing to their line manager's manager stating the grounds for appeal, which must be received within seven calendar days of receiving the decision letter. The appeal is normally heard by that manager (or an equivalent-level manager not previously involved), with at least seven calendar days' written notice of the hearing date. The employee may be accompanied by a trade union representative or workplace colleague. The appeal decision is final, with no further right of appeal.
notes: Grounded in §4.5. Two separate seven-day windows (to lodge the appeal, and notice of the hearing) that are easy to conflate, plus the finality of the outcome.

question: Can a manager trial a flexible working arrangement before agreeing to it permanently, and for how long?
expected_answer_summary: Yes. The manager must meet the employee to discuss it first, and the trial length is agreed between them — the policy recommends between 3 and 6 months. If successful it can be confirmed formally in writing; if not, further discussions about alternatives should take place.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.2. The 3-6 months is a recommendation, not a limit — NM-021 tests that distinction directly.

question: What happens to an on-call commitment if an employee reduces their hours through flexible working?
expected_answer_summary: If the role includes an on-call requirement that is continuing, it is undertaken on a pro rata basis where the flexible working request results in fewer hours being worked.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.2. A cross-policy hook: UHN-PO-HR07 §4.4 separately explains how part-time on-call PAY is adjusted proportionally, so the two policies dovetail — see SY-018.

question: Does a request to work from home need to be made formally?
expected_answer_summary: Not necessarily. Home or hybrid working can be agreed informally through discussion with the line manager. But changing the nominated base of work as stated in the contract of employment must be done formally, as must any change that alters the contract.
notes: Grounded in §4.3.1. The informal/formal boundary is defined by contractual effect, not by subject matter — a distinction a system is likely to flatten into a simple yes or no.

question: How should a manager handle several flexible working requests received at the same time?
expected_answer_summary: Consider them in the order received, each on its own merits against operational and service needs — the manager is not required to judge which request is most deserving. Requests must not be discussed with other affected colleagues without permission. If existing flexible arrangements are blocking new ones, the manager can call for volunteers among staff already working flexibly to adjust their arrangements.
notes: Grounded in §4.4. The explicit 'not required to make a judgement about the most deserving request' instruction is unusual and easy to contradict — a system reasoning from general fairness intuitions will likely produce the opposite advice.

question: How often must DBS checks be renewed for Trust staff?
expected_answer_summary: Every three years as a minimum, or at the point an employee changes roles within the Trust where the required DBS level has changed. Agency workers are different — they need a check once a year.
notes: Grounded in §1 and §8. The agency-worker exception (annual, not three-yearly) sits several sections away from the general rule and is the part most likely to be missed.

question: Who pays for a new starter's DBS check?
expected_answer_summary: The employee. New starters (and staff changing roles, from 01 February 2019) pay for the disclosure application or DBS Update Service subscription, deducted from their first pay. If an employee lets their Update Service registration lapse, they are responsible for the full cost of re-registering and of a new DBS check.
notes: Grounded in §3 and §5. A cost-allocation question where the amount is deliberately never stated — see NM-024.

question: Do doctors on rotational training schemes need a new DBS check each time they move Trust?
expected_answer_summary: No. Doctors on educationally approved rotational training schemes are treated as being in continuous employment, so they need a DBS check every three years rather than at each rotation. They must still produce their current certificate to the Recruitment Team for an authenticity check.
notes: Grounded in §7. A group-specific exception to the general rule — tests whether the system applies the right rule to the right staff group.

question: Can someone start work before their DBS disclosure comes back?
expected_answer_summary: Not in 'regulated activity'. In exceptional circumstances a risk-based assessment can allow it, provided the DBS disclosure has been applied for, the individual is not working with children, and safeguards are in place. Where someone is not in regulated activity but has patient access, a signed risk assessment is held on file until the check arrives.
notes: Grounded in §5.1. A conditional answer with three cumulative safeguards; a flat 'no' or a flat 'yes' both lose important detail.

question: Which trade unions does the Trust formally recognise?
expected_answer_summary: Ten: UNISON, the British Association of Occupational Therapists (BAOT), the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), the Royal College of Midwives (RCM), the Society of Radiographers (SoR), UNITE, the British Medical Association (BMA), the British Dental Association (BDA), the Chartered Society of Physiotherapists (CSP), and the Guild of Healthcare Pharmacists.
notes: Grounded in §2. A ten-item list that also appears as a signature block at the end of the document, so there are two retrievable copies — a good check on whether the system produces the complete set.

question: How often does the Joint Consultation and Negotiation Committee meet, and what counts as a quorum?
expected_answer_summary: Not less than four times a year, with special meetings by agreement on a minimum of 10 working days' notice. A quorum is no less than 50% of the persons entitled to be present on each side; nominated deputies count towards it, but co-opted members do not.
notes: Grounded in §11. Three interlocking facts, including the co-opted-members exclusion which is stated in a different sub-paragraph from the quorum rule itself.

question: How can the trade union recognition agreement be terminated, and is it legally binding?
expected_answer_summary: Either side can terminate it by giving 6 months' notice in writing. The agreement is not intended to be legally enforceable by either side and is binding in honour only.
notes: Grounded in §13. The 'binding in honour only' status is a substantive legal point that a system summarising loosely is likely to drop or contradict.

question: What charge does the Trust apply for processing trade union subscriptions through payroll?
expected_answer_summary: 0.5% of the subscriptions, under the check-off system where the employer deducts union subscriptions from salaries and pays them to the union monthly with a schedule of payment. The charge is subject to regular review.
notes: Grounded in §12. One of very few actual percentages in this document, and the only place in the corpus where a union subscription cost of any kind is quantified — contrast with NM-016, where the staff lottery deduction is named but never priced.

question: How long does basic pay protection last for an employee with six years' service?
expected_answer_summary: Three years — the 'at least five years' service band. The full scale is: up to one year → three months; at least one but under two years → six months; at least two but under five years → 12 months; at least five years → three years.
notes: Grounded in §4.1. Note the document contains a SECOND, different protection table for enhancements (§4.2) where five-plus years gives only 12 months. Retrieving the wrong table produces a confidently wrong answer with a real citation — SY-019 tests that confusion head-on.

question: What is 'Mark Time' in the pay protection policy?
expected_answer_summary: The rate of earnings is preserved without the benefit of any increments, pay awards or annual pay increases. The mark time salary is the salary received immediately before the change in role and pay. If the new post's maximum rises above the mark time figure through pay awards, the employee moves to that new maximum and the protection period ends.
notes: Grounded in §5 Definitions plus the mechanism in §4.1. The 'protection period ends early if pay awards overtake it' consequence lives in a different section from the definition.

question: Does an employee have a contractual right to pay protection?
expected_answer_summary: No. §3 states plainly that employees do not have a contractual right to pay protection. The policy also excludes bank workers, agency workers and self-employed contractors entirely.
notes: Grounded in §3. A single flat sentence that contradicts what most readers would assume from the rest of the document's detailed entitlement tables.

question: How long is excess travel protection paid for after a change of work base?
expected_answer_summary: Four years. The excess is calculated on bus fares or standard rail travel, or for private motor vehicle on the Reserve rate in Section 17 of the Agenda for Change Terms and Conditions Handbook.
notes: Grounded in §4.2. The four-year period is much longer than any of the basic-pay or enhancement protection periods in the same document, which makes it a distinctive fact worth isolating.

question: An employee with seven years' service is redeployed to a lower band and also loses their regular night-shift enhancement. How long is each part of their pay protected?
expected_answer_summary: Different periods for each: basic pay is protected for three years (the 'at least five years' band in §4.1), while the enhancement is protected for only 12 months (the 'at least five years' band in §4.2). The enhancement also only qualifies if it was regularly paid for at least six of the last 12 months, and the protected enhancement amount is frozen, non-pensionable, and does not count towards overtime.
notes: The sharpest question in this batch: the same service length maps to two DIFFERENT protection periods depending on which pay element is at stake, and the two tables look nearly identical. A system that retrieves one table and applies it to both halves gives a confidently wrong answer. Kept as a single-document entry because both tables are in one policy, but it is genuinely multi-chunk. Reclassified from answerable_synthesis to answerable_single: multi-chunk but single-document, and this eval reserves the synthesis category for cross-document questions.

question: A nurse with four years' service is moving to a new role within the Trust that involves working with a different vulnerable group. Do they need a new DBS check, and who pays?
expected_answer_summary: Yes — working with a different vulnerable group requiring a check against one or both barred lists is an explicit trigger for a new check (§6). As a staff member changing roles as part of the recruitment process, they pay for the disclosure application or Update Service subscription themselves (§3).
notes: Requires matching a scenario against a six-item trigger list and then connecting it to the separate cost-allocation rule. The four-years detail is a distractor — it does not affect the outcome, since the vulnerable-group change is independently sufficient. Reclassified from answerable_synthesis to answerable_single: multi-chunk but single-document, and this eval reserves the synthesis category for cross-document questions.

question: How long is the probationary period for a new employee, and what notice applies during it?
expected_answer_summary: Six months for every new member of staff except training doctors. Employment may be terminated during probation at any point by one week's notice on either side.
notes: Grounded in §5.1 and §5.9. The training-doctor exclusion and the symmetrical one-week notice are both easy to omit.

question: Can a probationary period be extended, and by how much?
expected_answer_summary: Yes, but only in exceptional circumstances, for no longer than 3 months, and only one extension will be granted. The manager must discuss it with their HR Manager/Advisor before telling the employee, and the extension must be confirmed in writing.
notes: Grounded in §6.7. The 'only one extension' limit is the constraint most likely to be dropped, and it changes the answer materially.

question: What probationary period applies to someone on a nine-month fixed-term contract?
expected_answer_summary: Four months, per the fixed-term table in §5.4 ('Up to 9 months → 4 months'). The full scale is: 3 months or less → 1 month; up to 6 months → 3 months; up to 9 months → 4 months; 12 months or more → 6 months.
notes: Grounded in §5.4. The table's heading row is chunked separately from the policy text that introduces it, so the figures arrive without their labels — a good test of whether the system can still map the right row.

question: Does an employee who transfers to a different role within the Trust have to serve a new probationary period?
expected_answer_summary: No — staff who transfer internally, take a secondment or are promoted are not subject to a new probationary period, unless they are still within their current one. But staff who previously worked for the Trust or held a bank position and are newly appointed ARE subject to probation.
notes: Grounded in §5.3. Two adjacent rules that point in opposite directions for superficially similar situations (internal move vs re-appointment from bank), which is exactly where a system is likely to over-generalise.

question: How is a job matched to a pay band under the job evaluation process, and who sits on the panel?
expected_answer_summary: The primary method is Job Matching against a nationally agreed profile, evaluating the role against 16 Factors. Panels must consist of at least two trained members from both Management and Staff Side. If the role is unique and cannot be matched to a National Profile, it is locally evaluated using a Job Analysis Questionnaire (JAQ). All panel outcomes are then consistency checked by a second panel with the same minimum composition.
notes: Grounded in §4.2 and §4.3. The '16 Factors' figure appears exactly once in the corpus.

question: What happens if a member of staff's professional registration lapses?
expected_answer_summary: They cannot be employed in their role until renewal is confirmed, so they are suspended from duty with NO pay for that period, and Payroll must be notified at once. A formal meeting follows under the Disciplinary Policy, with written warning beforehand that a disciplinary sanction is a possible outcome, and the manager writes to confirm the outcome within 5 working days. A second consecutive failure to renew can lead to dismissal. Reinstatement on re-registration requires it to happen within two days of expiry, though managers have discretion to extend in exceptional circumstances only.
notes: Grounded in §7.3. A severe, multi-step consequence chain — unpaid suspension is the headline and the two-day reinstatement window is the detail most likely to be lost.

question: What are the conditions for protecting pensionable pay when stepping down to a lower-paid role before retirement?
expected_answer_summary: The employee must be over the minimum retirement age, must apply for the new role through the normal Recruitment and Selection process, must protect their pensionable pay within one month of the change, and must take at least a 10% drop in pay for a minimum of 12 months. NHS Pensions should be contacted for guidance.
notes: Grounded in the 'Step Down' section §5. Four cumulative conditions including a counter-intuitive one — the employee must take a big enough pay cut (at least 10%) to qualify, which reads backwards from how protections usually work.

question: What happens if someone raises a request for resolution that turns out to be malicious?
expected_answer_summary: If investigation gives reason to believe a request was raised with vexatious or malicious intent — meaning unreasonable, without foundation, and made to cause upset or hurt — it is taken seriously and the person making the request may be subject to formal disciplinary action.
notes: Grounded in §4.7 'Vexatious or Malicious Requests for Resolution'. Includes the policy's own definition, which sets a high bar (all three of unreasonable, without foundation, and intended to hurt) that a loose answer will understate.

question: How long is the consultation period for an organisational change?
expected_answer_summary: Usually 30 days. Where there is no major change — that is, no potential redundancies — the period may be reduced by agreement with the affected staff and their union representatives. Where statutory timescales apply, consultation continues for as long as those require.
notes: Grounded in §4.8. A default with two different override routes in opposite directions (shorter by agreement, longer if statute demands), so a bare '30 days' is incomplete.

question: In what circumstances would an employee lose their entitlement to a redundancy payment?
expected_answer_summary: If they unreasonably refuse suitable alternative employment. Specifically, if they obtain, are offered, or unreasonably refuse to apply for or accept suitable alternative employment with the Trust or another NHS employer, and that employment starts within 4 weeks of their termination date, they are not eligible — and any redundancy payments already made become repayable.
notes: Grounded in §6.1 and §6.3. The 4-week window and the clawback of payments already made are both concrete and easily missed.

question: Who is entitled to raise a concern under the Freedom to Speak Up policy?
expected_answer_summary: Anyone who works in NHS healthcare — healthcare professionals, non-clinical workers, receptionists, directors, managers, contractors, volunteers, students, trainees, junior doctors, locum, bank and agency workers, and former workers.
notes: Grounded in §4.3. Deliberately broad list including two groups a system is likely to omit: contractors and FORMER workers. The policy's breadth is the substance of the answer, so a truncated list materially understates it.

question: What is the difference between speaking up confidentially and anonymously?
expected_answer_summary: Confidentially means revealing your identity to the person you speak to on condition they will not share it without your consent — your name is known only to the FTSU Guardian, which allows a response and learning outcomes to be shared back with you. Anonymously means not revealing your identity to anyone at all (via pseudonymous email, voicemail or letter); this is always respected and does not affect whether the concern is investigated, but it limits the ability to report back to you.
notes: Grounded in the 'Confidentially Speaking Up' and 'Anonymously' sections. A definitional distinction that is routinely conflated in ordinary usage, so a system relying on general knowledge rather than the document is likely to blur them.

question: Who pays a seconded employee's salary during a secondment to an external host organisation?
expected_answer_summary: The Trust retains the employee on the KGH payroll and continues to pay them, then recharges the salary to the host employer for reimbursement. Pay awards and annual increments still apply and the original incremental date is unchanged (or adjusted per AfC rules if temporarily promoted). Staff seconded IN from an external organisation normally stay on their substantive employer's payroll.
notes: Grounded in §5.2. The direction of travel matters — who pays differs depending on whether the employee is seconded out or in — and the recharge mechanism is the detail that distinguishes a correct answer from a vague one.

question: How much notice is required to end a secondment early?
expected_answer_summary: A minimum of one month's notice, other than in exceptional circumstances. Early termination must be agreed by both the seconding and the host manager/organisation, and the employee must notify their substantive employer without delay and be available for work under their substantive contract.
notes: Grounded in §5.7. The bilateral-agreement requirement is as important as the notice period — one party cannot simply end it.

question: How do I contact a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian?
expected_answer_summary: By email or phone to the site inbox: NGH is ngh-tr.raising.concerns@nhs.net and KGH is kgh-tr.kghfreedomtospeak@nhs.net (also cited as kgh-tr.freedomtospeak@nhs.net), each with an associated FTSU phone line. The Guardians work across both hospitals and have access to both inboxes, so someone with a group-wide concern may use either. Individual Guardian contact details are on the staff intranet, and there is an anonymous reporting form for both trusts.
notes: Grounded in §4.4 and §4.5. Worth noting the document gives the KGH address two different ways (kgh-tr.kghfreedomtospeak@nhs.net in one section, kgh-tr.freedomtospeak@nhs.net in another) — a genuine internal inconsistency in the source. A high-quality answer would ideally surface both rather than silently pick one. This was originally drafted as a near-miss assuming no contact details existed; the corpus check found them, along with the inconsistency, so it became an answerable question instead.

question: What pre-employment checks must be completed before someone starts work at the Trust?
expected_answer_summary: Set in line with NHS Employers and Care Quality Commission standards, and including (but not limited to): verification of identification, right to work, employment history, work health assessment, DBS check where applicable, professional registration and qualification checks where applicable, Health Professionals Alert Notice (HPAN) check where applicable, and Fit and Proper Person check where applicable. An unconditional offer should only follow once these are met, and candidates who fail to provide satisfactory checks may have their offer withdrawn.
notes: Grounded in §5.7 and §5.8. An eight-item list with a 'not limited to' qualifier and four 'where applicable' conditions — a complete answer has to convey that the list is neither exhaustive nor uniformly mandatory. Also note §5.7 allows consideration where checks are hard to obtain for age-related reasons (e.g. school leavers with no ID verification), provided it is documented.

question: According to the Maintaining High Professional Standards policy, what section number covers 'Part I: Action When a Concern Arises'?
expected_answer_summary: Section 4.1, per the current policy (UHN-PO-HR26, effective May 2027). The superseded prior version (B1.1, filename marked SUPERSEDED) numbers the identical content as section 10.1 — a system that answers '10.1' is citing the stale document.
notes: B1.1 and UHN-PO-HR26 are the same policy lineage, old vs current (this exact pair is already used in tests/test_corpus.py to prove section numbering isn't hardcoded). B1.1's own filename is marked SUPERSEDED, and UHN-PO-HR26's own cover-sheet Supersedes field explicitly names 'Policy B.1.1 – KGH' (verified via intake.py's parse_cover_sheet, not just the filename) — so the stale/current relationship is grounded in document metadata both ways, not assumed. A correct system should ground its answer in the current document and, ideally, note the earlier document exists and disagrees, rather than silently averaging or picking whichever ranks higher in retrieval.

question: What is the current weekly rate of Statutory Sick Pay?
expected_answer_summary: £123.25 a week (or 80% of average weekly earnings if lower), per the current GOV.UK page. The 2025 Wayback Machine snapshot of the same page states £116.75 (an older rate) with slightly different wording (no '80% of earnings' clause) — a system that answers with the older figure is citing a stale archived snapshot rather than the current source.
notes: Both PDFs are literally the same GOV.UK page: 'Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) - GOV.UK.pdf' is the current page (timestamped 2026, no archive banner); 'Print Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) 2025 - GOV.UK.pdf' carries a visible 'The Wayback Machine' banner and is an archived January 2025 snapshot. Confirmed by reading both §2 chunks directly: £123.25 vs £116.75. Also confirmed the non-'2025' Maternity/Paternity/Shared-Parental-Leave pages are genuinely current (no Wayback banner, 2026 timestamp) — the same current-vs-archived pattern likely holds across all four GOV.UK topic pairs, not just SSP, which is worth exploiting for more contradictory_stale questions in a later batch.

question: What is the current statutory weekly rate of Statutory Maternity Pay after the first six weeks?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
distractor_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £194.32 a week, or 90% of average weekly earnings if lower, for the 33 weeks after the first 6. The 2025 archived snapshot of the same page says £184.03 — a system answering with that figure is citing a stale Wayback Machine capture.
notes: Same current-vs-archived pattern as CS-002, confirmed by diffing the two PDFs: identical page structure, different rate. The archived copy is identifiable by its Wayback Machine URLs (/web/20240930171915/...) embedded throughout the body text, which is a signal a retrieval system could in principle learn to use.

question: What is the current statutory weekly rate of Paternity Pay?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
distractor_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £194.32, or 90% of average weekly earnings if lower. The 2025 archived snapshot states £184.03.
notes: Confirmed by diff: the only substantive change in the Pay section between the two captures is the rate. Note the archived filename has no space before the hyphen ('2025- GOV.UK'), unlike the maternity pair ('2025 - GOV.UK') — the doc_ids here are exact and were copied from the chunker's output rather than typed.

question: Can Paternity Leave be split into two separate one-week blocks, and how long after the birth can it be taken?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
distractor_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: Yes — under the current page, up to 2 weeks can be taken together or separately in one-week blocks, and leave must end within 52 weeks of the birth. The 2025 archived page describes a superseded regime for babies due on or before 6 April 2024 under which leave had to be taken 'in one go' and had to end within 56 days of the birth.
notes: The most substantive stale-content trap in the statutory set: this is a genuine rule change, not just a repriced figure, and the archived page states BOTH the old and new regimes side by side under date conditions. A system retrieving the archived page can produce a confidently wrong 'you must take it in one go' answer with a real citation behind it. 56 days vs 52 weeks is also a large enough gap to be unmistakable in scoring.

question: What is the minimum average weekly earnings threshold for qualifying for Statutory Maternity Pay and Statutory Paternity Pay?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
distractor_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave 2025 - GOV.UK
Print Paternity pay and leave 2025- GOV.UK
expected_answer_summary: £129 a week for both. The 2025 archived snapshots of both pages say £123.
notes: Deliberately spans two current documents with two matching archived distractors, so a system can get this half-right by mixing a current page with an archived one and returning two different thresholds for what is in fact a single shared figure. Inconsistency between the two halves of the answer is itself the signal of stale retrieval.

question: Are the first three days of sickness absence paid under Statutory Sick Pay?
expected_answer_summary: Yes — the current page says SSP is paid 'for all the full days you're off sick that you normally would have worked', with no waiting period. The 2025 archived snapshot describes the superseded rule under which the first 3 working days were unpaid.
notes: A second genuine rule change (not a repricing) in the SSP pair, independent of the rate change already covered by CS-002. Confirmed by reading both: the archived text says 'except for the first 3' and refers to a 'waiting period', language absent from the current page. No distractor_doc_ids field because the stale content and the correct grounding are the same document — which is precisely why this question tests something the other contradictory_stale questions cannot. question: Why does the ID badge policy allow staff to keep their badge as a souvenir after they leave the Trust?
notes: False premise: a13 §8 requires the opposite — on leaving, staff must hand the badge to their line manager, who securely destroys it and notifies Identity Services to remove system access. A correct answer should reject the premise, not explain a policy of letting staff keep badges.

question: Why does the career break policy guarantee full annual leave accrual while staff are on a break?
notes: False premise: a36 §6 states explicitly there is NO entitlement to annual leave (or occupational sick pay or other discretionary entitlements) while on a career break. The premise is the exact opposite of the documented policy.

question: Why is the 96% attendance requirement for the additional leave purchase scheme a strict, non-negotiable threshold?
notes: False premise: a38 §5 explicitly says the 96% figure is an 'ideal' minimum 'subject to the line manager's discretion' — the opposite of a strict, non-negotiable rule. Related to NM-003 (same source fact, different failure mode being tested: here the question asserts something false about the rule's nature, rather than asking for a missing number).

question: Why does Statutory Maternity Pay continue for the full 52 weeks of maternity leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: leave is 52 weeks but SMP is paid for up to 39 weeks only (§3 'Pay'). The question fuses two real figures from the same document into a claim the document contradicts. A correct answer should separate the two durations rather than explain a 52-week pay entitlement.

question: Why is Paternity Leave only available to employees who have completed 26 weeks of continuous employment?
expected_doc_ids: Print Paternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: Paternity Leave is available from the first day of employment; the 26-week continuous-employment test applies to Paternity Pay, not leave. The document states both facts a few lines apart, so this tests whether the system keeps the leave/pay distinction rather than collapsing it.

question: Why do employees stop accruing holiday entitlement while they are on Statutory Maternity Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: §1 'Employment rights when on leave' lists the right to 'build up (accrue) holiday' as expressly protected during Statutory Maternity Leave. The premise asserts the exact opposite of a bulleted statement in the source.

question: Why does Statutory Maternity Leave require a minimum length of service with your employer?
expected_doc_ids: Print Maternity pay and leave - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: §4 says 'It does not matter how long you've been with your employer, how many hours you work or how much you get paid.' The 26-week requirement that the question is reaching for belongs to SMP, not maternity leave — the same leave/pay confusion as FP-005, tested from the maternity side.

question: Why are employers allowed to pay part-time staff less than the statutory minimum rate of Statutory Sick Pay?
notes: False premise: §1 states plainly 'You cannot get less than the statutory amount.' Nothing in the document creates a part-time exception. Tests resistance to a premise that sounds administratively plausible.

question: Why is Shared Parental Leave limited to a maximum of two separate blocks?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: §6 says up to 3 separate blocks each, and more than 3 if the employer agrees. The question asserts a lower, wrong cap — close enough to the real number that a system matching loosely on 'blocks of leave' may accept it.

question: Why do SPLIT days and KIT days count towards the same 10-day total?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: the SPL page states SPLIT days (20 each) are 'in addition to the 10 keeping in touch (KIT) days' — two separate allowances, not one shared pool. The premise takes the real 10-day KIT figure and misapplies it to both.

question: Why must a mother return to work before her partner is allowed to begin Shared Parental Leave?
expected_doc_ids: Print Shared Parental Leave and Pay - GOV.UK
notes: False premise: §5 'When you can start' says 'You can start SPL while your partner is still on maternity or adoption leave as long as they've given binding notice to end it.' Returning to work is one of two alternatives, not a precondition — the question promotes an either/or into a requirement.

question: Why can Trust employees split their maternity leave into several separate blocks?
notes: False premise: §4.1.4 states 'You must take your maternity leave all in one go, you cannot break or split your maternity leave.' The same prohibition is repeated for adoption leave in §4.3.3. Splittable leave IS a real feature of this policy — but of shared parental leave and paternity leave, not maternity — so the premise borrows a true fact from a neighbouring section.

question: Why do Bank Workers need to complete 12 months' service before they can take maternity leave at the Trust?
notes: False premise on two counts: §4.1.4 gives the right to 52 weeks' maternity leave 'regardless of length of service or if you are in a contracted post or a Bank Worker', and the 12-month test is for Occupational Maternity PAY, from which Bank Workers are excluded entirely. The question fuses a real number with the wrong entitlement and the wrong staff group — a good answer has to separate leave from pay and note the Bank Worker exclusion.

question: Why does the Trust refuse all requests for continuous Shared Parental Leave that exceed six weeks?
notes: False premise: §4.4.2 says the opposite — 'You have a right to take continuous leave, and we will not refuse these requests.' The six-week figure is lifted from the section's own worked example ('a request for six weeks in a row'), which makes the fabricated threshold look grounded. It is discontinuous leave that can be refused, never continuous.

question: Why is Neonatal Care Leave paid at the Statutory Maternity Pay rate at this Trust?
notes: False premise, and unusually well-disguised: §4.1.9 does say 'Under the Neonatal Act the provision for pay is at the same rate as Statutory Maternity Pay' — so the premise is quotable from the document. But the very next sentence says 'However, we have decided to retain our previous provision of paying this leave at full pay.' A system that stops reading one sentence early will confidently confirm a false premise with a genuine citation. Pairs with SY-013, which asks the same thing the right way round.

question: Why must an employee return to work full-time for 12 months after maternity leave to keep their Occupational Maternity Pay?
notes: False premise: the OMP table in §4.1.5 requires an intention to return to NHS work in a substantive post for at least 3 months, not 12, and says nothing about returning full-time. The question inflates the duration and invents a hours condition, while 12 months is a real number elsewhere in the same table (the continuous-service test) — so both wrong components are individually retrievable.

question: Why must an employee complete 26 weeks of service before they can request flexible working?
notes: False premise: §4.4 states the right to request agile/flexible working is a 'day one' right with no qualifying period. The 26-week figure is real elsewhere in the corpus — it is the continuous-service test for SMP, SAP and ShPP in UHN-PO-HR10 and on the GOV.UK pages — so it is a number a retrieval system can find and misattribute.

question: Why does the Trust refuse flexible working requests from staff who already have an existing flexible arrangement?
notes: False premise: no such rule exists. §4.4 describes something adjacent but different — where existing arrangements make a NEW colleague's request unworkable, the manager may ask for volunteers among those already working flexibly to adjust their arrangements. The policy nowhere bars someone with an existing arrangement from requesting another; indeed it permits more than one request per 12 months. The premise inverts who is affected by the existing-arrangements clause.

question: Why are bands 8 and 9 excluded from on-call call-out payments?
notes: False premise: §4.5 says the opposite in a single explicit sentence — 'There is no disqualification from this payment for bands 8 and 9, as a result of being called out.' The premise is plausible enough (senior-grade exclusions do exist in some NHS pay arrangements) that a system reasoning from background knowledge rather than the document is likely to confirm it.

question: Why is compensatory rest paid at time and a half?
notes: False premise: §4.11 states compensatory rest is UNPAID rest given like-for-like to replace a missed break. Time and a half is a real rate in the same document (§4.5, for call-out work), so the question welds a genuine figure onto the one entitlement it does not apply to — a system retrieving both sections and merging them carelessly will produce exactly this error.

question: Why does an employee receive a full 12-hour day in lieu for being on-call over a public holiday?
notes: False premise: §4.7 specifies TOIL equivalent to the day they would have worked — 'e.g. this would be a 7.5 hour day not a whole on-call period of 12 or 24 hours'. The document anticipates this exact misconception and rules it out in a parenthetical, so a system that confirms the premise has retrieved the right passage and misread its most important clause.

question: Why does the Trust pay for its employees' DBS checks?
notes: False premise: a12 places the cost squarely on the employee in three separate places (§3, §5, and the lapsed-registration rule in the Managers' responsibilities). The premise is a natural assumption — most employers do fund these — which is what makes it a good test of document-grounding over prior expectation.

question: Why is the trade union recognition agreement legally enforceable against the Trust?
notes: False premise: §13 states 'The agreement is not intended to be legally enforceable by either side and is binding in honour only.' The document cites real legislation elsewhere (the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, s.178), which lends the premise false plausibility — a system that spots statutory references may infer enforceability the agreement expressly disclaims.

question: Why does pay protection continue indefinitely once it has been awarded?
notes: False premise: every form of protection in this policy is time-limited (three months to three years for basic pay, three to twelve months for enhancements, four years for excess travel), and §4.1 gives two ways it can end EARLY — if pay awards lift the new post's maximum above the mark time figure, or if the employee unreasonably refuses a suitable comparable post. Indefinite protection is the one thing the policy never provides.

question: Why can an employee be given pay protection when moving two bands below their current post?
notes: False premise: §4.1 restricts it explicitly — 'Pay protection will only be offered for redeployment to a post limited to one band below the existing substantive post.' A single-word difference (one vs two) from the real rule, which makes it a precision test rather than a plausibility test.

question: Why must an employee have proof of wrongdoing before raising a Freedom to Speak Up concern?
